title: Do we need two full circles to find the top point?
description: The top point of the house is found where two circles cross, and the video asks whether both full circles are needed. Keeko's doubt is that two full circles are needed to be sure, and the video breaks it.
teaching_notes: One idea: only the small parts of the circles near the crossing matter, so short arcs are enough. Watch for students who think a construction is wrong unless the circles are complete.

source: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A
video_script.why: A learner sees that the crossing point of two circles is found from small arcs alone, which saves time and keeps the drawing clean.
video_script.substitution: the book's two circles of radius five centimetres centred at B and at C, replaced by two short arcs
video_script.anchor: the book's house with two circles of radius 5 cm from B and C crossing at the top point A
video_script.wrong_answer: we need two full circles to be sure
video_script.wrong_move: believes a complete circle must be drawn before the crossing point can be trusted
video_script.payoff_line: No, short arcs of radius five centimetres from bee and from cee are enough.

final_answer.value: No; short arcs of radius 5 cm from B and from C that cross at A are enough
final_answer.spoken: no, short arcs from bee and from cee that cross at eigh are enough

maths_rules: the point A is where the two circles cross
only the small parts of the circles near the crossing are needed
an arc of radius 5 cm from B and an arc of radius 5 cm from C cross at the same point A
video_script.design: Two full circles are drawn and the crossing point is marked. Most of each circle then fades, and only two short arcs through the crossing stay.
